candidateRows: Ordinary moral discourse presupposes that moral wrongness is independent of preferences, conventions, beliefs, and practices.
This establishes the commonsense conception of moral objectivity that supplies the starting point for Enoch's defense of robust realism.
Enoch uses the wrongness of humiliating people to distinguish ordinary objective moral claims from claims constituted by social convention or individual attitudes.
Once commonsense moral objectivity is accepted, realism is the default position and opponents bear the burden of defeating it.
The move allocates the dialectical burden and links stance-independent moral truth directly to a realist ontology of irreducible normative facts.
Enoch argues that truths independent of human responses naturally look like facts involving wrongness and should remain the default unless objections succeed.
Normative truths gain ontological respectability because belief in them is indispensable to deliberation, as electrons are indispensable to explanation.
This supplies Enoch's affirmative argument for normative facts rather than relying solely on commonsense objectivity and rebuttal of objections.
The argument analogizes deliberative indispensability to explanatory indispensability and concludes that indispensable normative truths and facts are ontologically respectable.
Realism may be easy to secure, yet metaphysical privilege cannot settle which rival stance-independent normative package should guide action.
This draws the debate's governing distinction between mind-independent moral facts and the stronger objectivity required to settle deliberation among rival packages.
Enoch's claim that stance-independent realist moral facts vindicate ordinary moral objectivity and support deliberation.
Clarke-Doane uses moral-twin cases to argue that rival properties can both be convention-independent, while higher-order privilege merely reproduces the question of which package to follow.
The rival-package challenge generalizes across normativity, and its iterative, apparently unintelligible scope supports treating it as misconceived rather than decisive.
Enoch directly answers the central objection by broadening its scope, defending metaphysical privilege, and challenging a presupposition behind the regress.
Clarke-Doane's argument that rival normative packages make metaphysical privilege unable to determine allegiance or settle deliberation.
Enoch distinguishes Clarke-Doane's stronger objectivity challenge from commonsense objectivity, extends it to rationality generally, and argues that its ubiquity suggests a defective framing.
Metaphysical privilege cannot settle deliberation: if privilege is nonnormative it is practically irrelevant, and if normative the rival-package regress returns.
The normative-or-nonnormative dilemma is the principal argument that realist metaphysical structure fails to provide action-guiding objectivity.
Enoch's proposal that sufficiently powerful metaphysics can privilege the correct normative package and expose the regress as misconceived.
After explaining that ethics should leave no deliberative gap once normative answers are known, Clarke-Doane argues that privilege is either an inert fact or another contested norm.
Normative privilege may also be metaphysical, and the recurrence of a rival privilege does not revive a genuine problem but only the original pseudo-problem.
This is Enoch's most direct response to the privilege dilemma and preserves his realist position by denying that iteration constitutes a substantive challenge.
Clarke-Doane's dilemma that nonnormative privilege is action-guidingly inert while normative privilege merely generates privilege-star.

Enoch accepts that privilege is normative and metaphysical, denies that iteration makes metaphysical progress necessary, and separates the general allegiance challenge from naturalist Twin Earth arguments.
A challenge shared by every remotely plausible metanormative view does not significantly count against realism absent an alternative that handles it better overall.
The move neutralizes the objection's comparative force by requiring Clarke-Doane to identify a superior alternative and assess positions holistically.
Clarke-Doane's contention that the rival-package problem undermines realism's capacity to vindicate normative objectivity.
Enoch argues that a ubiquitous challenge strengthens suspicion about the challenge itself and cannot discriminate among theories without a comparatively better alternative.
A metaethical theory need not be capable of persuading every confused or skeptical agent what to do; truth and plausibility are the relevant constraints.
This rejects the deliberative rescue demand underlying Clarke-Doane's objection and narrows what successful vindication must require from a theory.
Clarke-Doane's demand for guidance about what to do even when reflection leaves an agent under the rival-package illusion.
Enoch compares the confused deliberator with a thoroughgoing skeptic and argues that theoretical adequacy does not require actually extracting every mistaken person from skepticism.
Noncognitivism handles rival normative candidates better because action permits no belief-like pluralism and identifies what one ought to do with deciding or prescribing action.
This supplies the requested comparative alternative and claims it closes the gap between normative judgment and action that realist rival-package cases expose.
Enoch's challenge to identify a metanormative alternative that performs better on the rival-package problem.
Clarke-Doane argues that rival truth-apt normative properties leave a further question of what to do, whereas deciding or prescribing one action excludes competing actions.
Non-cognitivism can accommodate common-sense objectivity only by accepting substantial additional commitments whose plausibility is uncertain.
The argument supplies a comparative theoretical cost for the principal alternative to realism, supporting realism even if the immediate deliberative challenge is not decisive.
Justin's suggestion that a non-cognitivist treatment can avoid the realist's difficulty about settling action.
After Justin distinguishes sufficiency from necessity, David broadens the comparison and argues that accommodating ordinary objectivity imposes further burdens on non-cognitivism.
Once a deliberating agent concludes in the first person that an action ought to be done, no further deliberative question normally remains to be settled.
This directly contests the claimed gap between knowing what one ought to do and settling what to do, which is the debate's central challenge to realist objectivity.
Justin's claim that rival normative properties leave an intelligible further question about what action to choose.
David distinguishes akratic action from unsettled deliberation and argues that exotic ought-star scenarios distort the ordinary first-person phenomenology of deciding.
A deflationary, attitude-centered form of non-cognitivism need not inherit the elaborate semantic machinery associated with standard expressivist theories.
The move protects the principal rival to realism from a comparative-cost objection, though it does not itself establish the deliberative gap at the center of the motion.
David's contention that non-cognitivism bears unattractive extra commitments in order to explain common-sense objectivity.
Justin concedes familiar non-cognitivist complications but sketches a different approach combining semantic deflationism with an account of the attitudes expressed.
Rare reflective disputes between rival logics show that knowledge of validity does not non-causally settle whether an inference should be made.
The counterexample generalizes the deliberative-distance argument beyond ethics and directly challenges the inference from ordinary phenomenology to normative facts settling deliberation.
David's phenomenological argument that concluding one ought to act normally leaves no further deliberative step.
Justin uses disputes over quantum logic and reflective inference to argue that unusual cases remain intelligible and cannot be dismissed because most agents never encounter them.
A theory pays a much smaller dialectical cost for an artificial treatment of rare reflective cases than for failing to explain central everyday deliberative practice.
This supplies the comparative methodology by which realism can survive the opponent's exotic counterexamples while retaining an advantage in explaining ordinary normative practice.
Justin's quantum-logic example offered to show that rare reflective cases undermine the appeal to ordinary phenomenology.
David accepts that exceptional cases need an account but argues that theoretical evaluation should weight failures according to the centrality of what requires explanation.
The centrality of a deliberative problem should be tested using agents who understand it, rather than inferred from its absence in an unreflective majority.
The move attacks the methodological basis for discounting the counterexamples and preserves their force against realism despite their rarity in ordinary deliberation.
David's claim that rarity and distance from everyday phenomenology substantially reduce the theoretical cost of the challenge.
Justin questions whether prevalence tracks philosophical importance and proposes examining deliberators who are actually aware of the rival-normativity problem.
A philosophical account may properly prioritize the central target practice and treat hyper-theoretical deviations with a localized error theory.
The analogy defends the criterion used to discount reflective edge cases and thus supports the broader realist reply to the deliberative-distance challenge.
Justin's proposal that reflective experts, rather than ordinary unreflective practice, determine whether the problem is central.
David compares his methodological emphasis to Blackburn's effort to accommodate ordinary normative discourse while setting aside unusually theoretical commitments.
Apparently baroque foundational anomalies cannot simply be assigned negligible weight, because they may reveal a defect that transforms an otherwise successful framework.
This denies the realist's proposed weighting of exceptional cases and reiterates that the unresolved deliberative distance applies to any fact, normative or otherwise.
David's methodology of prioritizing ordinary target practice and discounting hyper-theoretical or arcane anomalies.
Justin argues that foundational puzzles can demand revision despite ordinary success, then asks what solution realism has to the persistent gap between facts and regulation of behavior.
The deliberative objection is an explanatory challenge rather than a contradiction, so its theoretical cost properly varies with the centrality of the phenomenon it concerns.
The response explains why the Russell analogy does not force wholesale rejection of realism and restores the comparative weighting central to the pro defense.
Justin's comparison of the deliberative-distance problem to Russell's paradox and other framework-transforming anomalies.
David grants that the challenge deserves an answer but argues that explanatory awkwardness about arcane cases costs less than failure regarding a central feature of practice.
Contradictions are themselves defeasible theoretical costs rather than categorically decisive failures, so they do not differ in kind from other explanatory anomalies.
By rejecting the categorical contrast on which David's reply relies, the move blocks his attempt to downgrade the deliberative challenge merely because it is non-contradictory.
David's distinction between contradiction and a merely explanatory challenge whose cost depends on practical centrality.
Justin appeals to paraconsistent logic to argue that even contradictions vary in practical and theoretical severity, placing them on a continuum with other anomalies.
A contradiction is not necessarily worse evidence against a theory than a highly implausible empirical prediction.
The comparison directly supports the con-side claim that apparent inconsistency need not supply a uniquely decisive stopping point unavailable in other theoretical disputes.
Enoch's question whether a contradiction must count as an especially bad theoretical consequence.
After denying that logic is categorically special, Clarke-Doane compares a set-theoretic contradiction with an evidentially unsupported prediction that the sun will become a black hole.
One may confidently reject Priest's position because there are no true contradictions.
The claim supplies the pro side with a case of justified philosophical confidence intended to distinguish decisive contradiction-based rejection from the disputed moral challenge.
Clarke-Doane's denial that contradictions are necessarily worse than other strongly unsupported consequences.
Following Clarke-Doane's refusal to rank contradictions as uniquely bad, Enoch appeals to confidence in rejecting Priest on the ground that no contradictions are true.
Rejecting true contradictions is distinct from the question whether paraconsistent logic is legitimate.
The distinction blocks an attempted inference from denying true contradictions to treating classical logic as uniquely mandatory or contradiction as automatically debate-ending.
Enoch's appeal to the falsity of true contradictions as grounds for confidently rejecting Priest.
Clarke-Doane interrupts the appeal to there being no true contradictions by separating dialetheism from the earlier issue concerning paraconsistent logical consequence.
Confidence about contradictions can mark a legitimate endpoint of argument, unlike the substantially weaker challenge pressed against moral objectivity.
This move reconnects the logical analogy to the debate's central issue by arguing that the challenge to moral realism lacks the exceptional force needed to defeat justified confidence.
Clarke-Doane's distinction between rejecting true contradictions and accepting paraconsistent logical methods.
Enoch says the distinction does not undermine his needed point: some commitments legitimately stop philosophical argument, while the challenge under discussion is not comparably strong.
